extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance from the MPEP on applying pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 (a),(e),(f),(g) and related rules for novelty, derivation, inventorship, antedating references, affidavits/declarations, and interference practice. Focuses on how examiners and practitioners should evaluate references, inventorship assertions, and proofs to overcome rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing date antedating by earlier foreign or provisional application
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing date can be antedated by an earlier foreign priority application or provisional application if 35 U.S.C. 119 is met and the foreign application or provisional application “supports” (conforms to 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, requirements) all the claims of the U.S. application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Gosteli. A prior application which was not copending with the application at issue cannot be used to antedate a reference (In re Costello). A terminal disclaimer does not overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection (e.g., In re Bartfeld). See MPEP § 706.02(b) for methods to overcome pre-AIA 102(e) rejections and MPEP § 715 for affidavit/declaration contents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of 37 CFR 1.131 vs 1.132 affidavits/declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 is not appropriate if the reference describes an inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own work. In that case, applicant must submit an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 715 and § 716.10 for contents and uses of 1.132 affidavits/declarations for antedating references. See MPEP § 706.02(l)(1) for rejections under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 and applicability of 103(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection by showing the reference describes the inventor's own work
rubrics_metrics.description: A pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection may be overcome by showing the disclosure in the patent, publication, or application publication is a description of the inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own previous work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a showing can be made by proving association (e.g., same assignee) and that the reference author or patentee learned of the inventor's invention from the inventor directly or indirectly (In re Mathews). In situations of differing named inventive entities (e.g., a sole inventor X then later a joint application X & Y), it must be proven that the joint invention was made first or was described earlier in the earlier filings (In re Land). Declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 by involved parties may be used but must be specific and not vague (In re Carreira).

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to show diligence or reduction to practice when reference is applicant's own work
rubrics_metrics.description: When the reference reflects an inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own work, evidence of diligence or reduction to practice does not need to be provided to establish that the inventor invented the subject matter disclosed in the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A showing that the reference disclosure arose from an inventor's work coupled with a showing of conception by the inventor before the filing date of the reference will overcome a pre-AIA 102(e) rejection. Submission of an affidavit under 37 CFR 1.132 by the inventor who conceived the subject matter is an acceptable means (In re DeBaun). Exhibits showing conception (e.g., drawings given to counsel) can support the declaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims in a reference do not prove inventorship of individual elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming of individual elements or subcombinations in a combination claim of the reference does not itself establish that the inventor or at least one joint inventor invented those elements if the elements/subcombinations are not separately claimed apart from the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence of combination claims is not evidence that the inventor invented individual elements or subcombinations unless those elements are separately claimed (In re DeBaun; In re Facius). Examiner should assess whether the reference separately claims the subelements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) requires complete conception and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivation requires that another party completely conceived the invention and communicated that conception to the alleged deriver prior to any date on which the deriver had knowledge of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication must enable one of ordinary skill in the art to construct and successfully operate the invention (Hedgewick v. Akers). Proof of derivation supports a 102(f) rejection; derivation determinations often involve whether one party derived an invention from another (Ex parte Kusko).

rubrics_metrics.name: Party alleging derivation need not prove actual reduction to practice or U.S. locus
rubrics_metrics.description: The party alleging derivation need not prove an actual reduction to practice, derivation of public knowledge, or that derivation occurred in this country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation need not be limited to public disclosures and the site of derivation need not be in the United States to bar a deriver from patenting (Scott v. Brandenburger; Ex parte Andresen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation (102(f)) vs priority (102(g)) — distinct inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivation addresses originality (who invented the subject matter) while priority addresses which party first invented the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although both focus on inventorship, derivation is about whether one party derived the invention from another; priority concerns dates of conception and reduction to practice and diligence (Price v. Symsek).

rubrics_metrics.name: 102(f) may apply when 102(a) and 102(e) are not available
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) does not require inquiry into relative dates and may be applicable where subsections (a) and (e) are not available as statutory grounds for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For references dated after the applicant's effective filing date, relative dates may still provide evidence that subject matter was derived from the inventor. Applicants may need to provide satisfactory 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits to rebut apparent inventorship issues (Ex parte Kusko; In re Katz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship must be correctly named and corrected when erroneous
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must correctly name the inventor(s) on U.S. applications; foreign applicants may misunderstand U.S. rules and need correction via 37 CFR 1.48 requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If determination shows the inventive entity named is incorrect and admissions are uncontroverted, a rejection should be made (see MPEP § 706.03(a) for rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115 and pre-AIA 102(f) for applicable applications). See MPEP § 602.01(c) et seq. for procedures to correct inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath/declaration requirements for named inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor, or each joint inventor of a claimed invention (except provisional filers), must execute an oath or declaration directed to the application, except as provided in 37 CFR 1.64.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 602.01(a)/(b) for requirements of inventor's oath/declaration for applications filed on or after and before September 16, 2012. For applications filed before Sept 16, 2012, pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.41(a)(1) defines inventorship by the oath/declaration filed under pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.63; parties executing an oath/declaration are presumed to be inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor must contribute to the conception of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The threshold question in determining inventorship is who conceived the invention; unless a person contributes to conception, he is not an inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice is generally irrelevant for inventorship except in simultaneous conception/reduction contexts. For chemical compounds, conception of specific claimed compounds is required; general knowledge of anticipated properties is insufficient (In re Hardee; Board of Education v. American Bioscience). One who merely suggests a desired result, not the means, is not a coinventor (Ex parte Smernoff). See MPEP §§ 2138.04–2138.05 for evidence needed to establish conception or reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual domination allows adoption of others' ideas/materials
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may consider and adopt ideas and materials derived from many sources so long as he maintains intellectual domination over making the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining intellectual domination includes directing testing, selecting or rejecting as the work proceeds; adoption of ideas/materials can still be derivation if adopted without such domination (Morse v. Porter; New England Braiding Co. v. A.W. Chesterton Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor not required to personally reduce the invention to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor is not required to physically reduce the invention to practice; reduction to practice may be performed by others on the inventor's behalf without destroying inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficulties arise distinguishing those who contributed conception from technicians who followed instructions. Where implementation does not require inventive skill, a lack of personal involvement in process steps does not defeat inventorship (Fritsch v. Lin; In re DeBaun).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for joint inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint inventors may apply for a patent jointly even if they did not physically work together, did not contribute the same amount, or did not contribute to every claim; each joint inventor must contribute to the conception of at least one claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be some 'quantum of collaboration or connection' (e.g., collaboration, common direction, one inventor seeing and building on another's report). A contributor to one claim suffices. Contributors of a disclosed means for a means-plus-function claim element are joint inventors for that claim unless contribution was merely a reduction to practice of a broader sole inventor concept (35 U.S.C. 116; Ethicon v. U.S. Surgical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) to preclude 102(f) or 102(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) states that subsection (f) of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 (and similarly (g)) will not preclude patentability where subject matter developed by another and the claimed invention were owned by the same person, subject to assignment to the same person, or involved a qualifying joint research agreement at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 706.02(l) and § 2146 for requirements of 103(c)(2) and (3). Inventorship 'by another' is generally where there are different inventive entities with at least one inventor in common; case law (e.g., Ex parte DesOrmeaux) provides examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) basis for ex parte rejection and interference practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) can form the basis for an ex parte rejection if (1) the subject matter was actually reduced to practice by another before the applicant’s invention, and (2) there was no abandonment, suppression, or concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception alone is not sufficient to qualify as prior art under 102(g); evidence of actual reduction to practice is required (Kimberly-Clark v. Johnson & Johnson). Filing an application is a constructive reduction to practice but generally does not show actual reduction to practice needed for a 102(g) ex parte rejection. Subject matter qualifying only under 102(g) may also be grounds for a 103 rejection (In re Bass). See MPEP § 2138 et seq. for interference and priority charts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference practice and the role of conception/reduction/diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (g) of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 is the basis of interference practice, determining priority of invention by considering conception, reduction to practice, and reasonable diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference is an inter partes proceeding involving pending applications/patents naming different inventors. In interferences, priority charts consider C = conception, R = reduction to practice (actual or constructive), Ra = actual reduction, Rc = constructive reduction, and TD = commencement of diligence. For 37 CFR 1.131 purposes, conception and reduction to practice of the reference to be antedated are treated as on the effective filing date of the domestic or foreign patent or the date of printed publication.
